props.title: What music works for the ceremony, cocktail hour and reception?

rows.text: The one stretch of the day where everyone - friends and family alike - are paying close attention to it. The music is exposed and the timing has to be precise. A guitarist or a violinist can play the prelude as your guests arrive, the processional and the recessional, and softly during the ring exchange if you'd like. Want to know more about how the different parts of the day come together, or how many songs each act needs? Learn more on our ceremony page.

This is the hour when the vibe turns from formal to slightly less so. As the couple leaves for photographs, guests stand with a first drink feeling out what kind of night is ahead. The venue may be turning ceremony seating into dinner tables behind a wall.

A duo covers the whole hour at a level guests talk freely over. Wondering what a duo plays, how many songs you'll need, or whether a duo is enough for your guest list? Find out on our cocktail hour page.

You want the dance floor to stay active for hours, and that's a DJ's job. An open-format DJ, who plays all kinds of music, can read the crowd from the first dance to the last song. Where a wedding wants live musicians for dinner and a DJ after it, that's easy with Signet. One contract.

props.html: “Our guests couldn’t stop talking about how amazing he was, and we loved how he read the crowd and kept everyone engaged. He went above and beyond to make our day special, even learning a few of our favorite songs just for us.”
props.by: Savannah H., an outdoor wedding, November 2025.

props.html: Not sure what to budget for wedding music? Our cost guide can help. Your cocktail hour duo can also play a Sunday brunch the morning after, or an engagement party months before the wedding.

props.title: What act to book for a wedding
props.lede: Four sizes of musical act can cover nearly every Colorado wedding, and the guest count influences that quite a bit. Each entertainment option is spec'd below with a link to their own page for more details.

rows.text: This is our smallest option, and a popular choice for a ceremony. A solo guitarist can play a processional without amplification in most indoor spaces. Learn more about our solo guitarist.

This is an upright bass and a guitar playing jazz standards, and it's our most common booking for a cocktail hour. The duo can play straight through dinner, and the trio adds soft brushed drums for a bigger space or a longer guest list, while staying quiet enough for easy conversation. Take a look at our jazz duo and trio.
The same footprint with the set turned toward singer-songwriter covers, for a wedding that wants the songs one notch more familiar than standards. Check out our acoustic duo and trio.
One Spanish guitarist is a lovely choice for the ceremony or the cocktail hour. If you'd like a full flamenco show, Dirty Flamenco plays as a trio.

props.html:
For a small sample of music some acts perform, check out the repertoire page.

Getting married in Colorado Springs? Our Colorado Springs wedding page covers the venues and the drive. You can also learn about the venues and sound rules for weddings in Boulder, Fort Collins, Vail and Telluride. Want jazz from the ceremony to the last dance? Check out our jazz band for weddings.

props.html: For whomever is running the schedule

Wedding dates get decided ten to twelve months out, and twelve to eighteen for a mountain venue or a fall Saturday. We see that music tends to be shopped for 9 to 14 months before the date.

Send a date and you get a yes or a straight no on an act's availability with more details and other recommendations should you desire them.

Most of a wedding's music questions are really timing questions, and those details are on the planners pages: Things like stage footprints, and power requirements, load-in and strike time. Want to see how each part of the day leads into the next? Take a look at our run of show page. For altitude, curfews and other mountain venue details, head to our mountain corridor page.
Our Preferred Vendor List has the photographers, planners, videographers, caterers, florists and venues we’d recommend to our own clients, each with a link to their site.

items.q: Can one booking cover the ceremony and the cocktail hour?
items.a: Yes, and it's the most common way to book it. The same musicians walk from the ceremony space to wherever cocktails are happening, on one contract, which also covers the gap while the couple is away for photographs. Signet Artists books wedding musicians across Denver and the Colorado mountains.

items.q: Do we need a band for the whole wedding?
items.a: Most Colorado weddings are better served with live musicians for the ceremony and the cocktail hour, where volume and attention need a person reading the crowd, and a DJ for the reception, where you want your dance floor to stay active for hours.

The ceremony and the cocktail hour are gentle enough that guests greet and easily talk over them without raising their voices. The reception plays like a dance floor, up to what the venue allows and the guests prefer

items.q: What paperwork comes with the booking?
items.a: A certificate of insurance naming the venue, and one itemized invoice come in the same email as the contract. A personal contact's mobile number is reachable from setup to strike.

items.q: Do you play outdoor weddings in Colorado?
items.a: Yes, and many of them are outdoors. Outdoors adds three requirements at any size: a covered, level and dry performance area, power run to it (depending on instrumentation), and a "move-indoors" call before the day.
